clue.text: Cask-makers' street, leading to Stalky and Co's isle

definitions.note: the possessive stands for what belongs to coopers, the wooden strips they bind into barrels

parts.note: in Kipling's Stalky & Co the boys' hideout on the cliff is christened 'the pleasant isle of Aves'

explanation.surface: Directions along the coopers' street that lead out to the schoolboys' island hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: Stalky & Co is Kipling's book of boarding-school stories; in 'In Ambush' Beetle names the boys' secret gorse-covered den on the cliff 'the pleasant isle of Aves'. 'leading to' just puts the street first.
explanation.definitionFit: Coopers build barrels from curved wooden strips held by hoops, so those planks are the cask-makers' material.

clue.text: This crawler never tells you anything straight!

definitions.text: This crawler never tells you anything straight!

parts.words: This crawler never tells you anything straight!
parts.note: a device that jumbles telephone speech so eavesdroppers hear nonsense, also a climbing plant or crawling motorbike

explanation.surface: Complaining about a sycophant who is never honest with you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crawler' suggests a toady; it is something that clambers, and 'never tells you anything straight' is a device that garbles speech for secrecy.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrambler garbles a transmitted message so it cannot be understood without decoding, and also names something that clambers.

clue.text: Some tale by keeper of books?

definitions.meaning: a story or report of events
what a bookkeeper produces, a financial record

explanation.surface: A story told by a librarian or a bookkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: An account is a narrative report, and also the financial statement a bookkeeper draws up.

clue.text: Having a belt round the middle, could be a riot in uniform

definitions.text: Having a belt round the middle

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are placed in the word for uniform

parts.note: equal means uniform, the same throughout

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters of a riot can become something else

explanation.surface: A riot breaking out among soldiers in uniform, each wearing a belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges A RIOT into TORIA, and 'in' puts it inside EQUAL. 'uniform' looks like clothing; it means even.
explanation.definitionFit: The equator girdles the Earth at its middle, so the adjective describes a band round the centre.

clue.text: Slice it about — in the mincer, that is to say

indicators.note: meat put in the mincer is chopped to bits, so these letters are minced into a new order

parts.note: c, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A cook's instruction to slice something and put it through the mincer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the mincer' mixes SLICE IT together with C (circa, 'about'). The answer is the Latin word glossed as 'namely', written sc. or scil.
explanation.definitionFit: Scilicet is a Latin adverb used to introduce an explanation, meaning namely.

clue.text: Tea a sailor can brew for a carrier

parts.note: char is informal British for tea
AB, able seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: brew suggests mixing up, so the letters of can are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A sailor brews a pot of tea for a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brew' fits the tea but shuffles CAN into ANC. A charabanc was an early open motor coach used for outings.
explanation.definitionFit: A charabanc was an open coach for taking parties on excursions, so it carried passengers.

clue.text: End of 3 climbs into hiding place

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the letters are read upwards, from the bottom
only the closing stretch of the word in 3-down is kept, the start dropped

parts.note: refers to the answer at 3-down

explanation.surface: Something at the tail of a line ascends to a secret den.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of 3' takes RIAL, the last four letters of 3-down's answer; 'climbs' turns it upward to give the answer, and 'into' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A lair is a wild animal's den, a hidden place to rest.

clue.text: Gable has one — a border decoration

parts.note: Clark Gable was the Hollywood film star
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An actor's house gable carries an ornament along its edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gable' looks like part of a roof; it is the actor's surname giving his first name. A border is a flower bed along a garden's edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarkia is an annual flowering plant, often grown in flower beds to brighten the garden.

clue.text: Solicitor run in — fishy!

indicators.note: the run is put in the solicitor's word, one item taking in another

parts.note: a tout solicits custom
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A lawyer arrested on suspicion: something smells off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' suggests a lawyer; it is someone touting for business, and 'run in' looks like an arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation points to a fish: the trout is a freshwater fish of the salmon family.

clue.text: Free tuition embraces such a case

indicators.note: the words free tuition hold the answer inside them, hugging it

explanation.surface: Getting lessons for nothing covers this kind of lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' suggests a lawsuit; it is a small container for needles and sewing kit.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles or cosmetics.

clue.text: He used to get a shilling for his subscription

definitions.text: He used to get a shilling for his subscription

parts.words: He used to get a shilling for his subscription
parts.note: a man who signed up for the army was once paid the King's shilling, so 'subscription' means enlisting, not paying a fee

explanation.surface: Someone who once got a shilling back for signing up to a magazine or club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subscription' suggests a magazine; here it is signing one's name to join up. Taking the King's shilling was the old token payment that bound a man to serve in the British army.
explanation.definitionFit: A new enlisted soldier took the King's shilling on joining, so the person who received it was a new army entrant.

clue.text: Trouble-maker has no right to get excited

indicators.note: the troublemaker's word is said to be without something, so a letter is taken out of it

parts.note: an agitator stirs up trouble

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser with no rights of their own still manages to get worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' only links the wordplay to the definition. The answer is a musical direction from Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitato is a musical direction asking for an agitated, restless performance, so it means excited.

clue.text: Peak distribution of tablets ' here?

parts.note: the tablets are the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, handed to Moses on a mountain, not pills

explanation.surface: Asking where the busiest time for handing out pills might be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peak distribution' looks like a busiest time and 'tablets' like pills; read instead as the mountain where the tablets of the Law were handed down in Exodus.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible Moses received the two stone tablets of the Commandments on this mountain in the Sinai peninsula.

clue.text: Take off the garment right away

indicators.note: the right is sent away, so that letter is dropped from the garment's word

parts.note: a skirt is a garment

explanation.surface: An order to remove a piece of clothing straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' looks like undressing; it means imitating, and 'right away' is not 'at once' but R leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: To take off someone is to mimic them, and a short comic sketch parodies its target.

clue.text: A wretched March looms for Miss Jean Brodie

indicators.note: wretched means in a sorry, broken state, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A grim spring month lies ahead for the famous Edinburgh teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss Jean Brodie is the teacher heroine of Muriel Spark's novel; 'A' and 'for' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's heroine is a strict, opinionated Edinburgh school teacher, an example of the type.

clue.text: Thinking, perhaps, of belonging to the side?

definitions.meaning: the word goes before 'thinking' in the phrase for inventive, sideways problem-solving
an adjective meaning to do with the sides of something

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a way of thinking belongs on the sidelines.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateral thinking is approaching a problem indirectly, and the adjective itself means sideways or at the flank.

clue.text: Willingly permit to remain inactive

parts.note: lief is an old word for willingly or gladly
to allow is to permit

explanation.surface: Gladly letting someone stay idle.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmland left unsown for a season rests, so the phrase means staying idle.

clue.text: Antique chair alterations must be taken into account

indicators.note: the scrambled letters are put inside the abbreviation, as one item is taken into another

parts.note: AC (a/c) is the abbreviation for account

indicators.note: alterations change the arrangement of the letters of chair

explanation.surface: Changes made to an old chair must be considered when it is valued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Antique' looks like an adjective for the chair but is the definition; 'alterations' is the anagram signal and 'taken into' the container signal, with 'must be' only linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Something antique belongs to a much earlier age, as does an old-fashioned word or object.

clue.text: Vehicle broken down? Get rid — it's a banger!

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: broken down suggests something smashed apart, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clapped-out car breaks down: scrap it, it's a wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banger' is British slang for an old car and for a sausage, fitting the broken-down vehicle; here it is something that goes bang. 'broken down' rearranges GET RID into TRIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge holds the charge for a gun, so it explodes when fired.

clue.text: Violent behaviour of the hump-backed generation

parts.note: a ramp is a hump in a road; 'backed' only says it stands behind, supporting what follows
an age is a generation or era

explanation.surface: Unruly conduct among a generation of hunchbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hump-backed' looks like one adjective describing the generation; the hump word simply comes first, with the generation after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rampage is a spell of wild, destructive conduct by a crowd or person.

clue.text: Many an unknown animal comes to an abrupt end

definitions.text: Many an unknown animal comes to an abrupt end

indicators.note: the word many is cut off sharply, losing its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
X is the usual algebraic unknown
a cat is an animal

explanation.surface: Lots of creatures nobody knows about suddenly die out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes to an abrupt end' cuts the Y from MANY, as the breed itself has no tail; 'an' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed from the Isle of Man is born without a tail, so its body stops short.

clue.text: Food the German turns into fish soup

parts.note: chow is slang for food
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: Some foreign dish is being made into a fish soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns into' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A chowder is a thick soup typically of clams or other seafood with potato.

clue.text: Verdi & Co somehow get unhitched

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters end up arranged by some unknown means

explanation.surface: The composer and his company split up in some fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhitched' is the opposite of 'getting hitched', slang for marrying.
explanation.definitionFit: To divorce is to end a marriage legally, the reverse of getting hitched.

clue.text: The company to go Scottish

definitions.meaning: a band or crew of people
in Scots dialect the verb meaning to go or walk

explanation.surface: A firm deciding to move north of the border.
explanation.definitionFit: A gang is a group of people working together, and in Scotland the same word is the verb for walking.

clue.text: Millet, perhaps, exhibits this texture

definitions.meaning: millet is a cereal crop, an example of a seed crop
the pattern of fibres in wood or a surface

explanation.surface: A painting by Millet showing off its fine surface finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Millet' looks like the French painter; it is the cereal. 'exhibits this' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Millet is a cereal seed, and the same word also means the fibre pattern or texture of a material.

clue.text: Wash the young Dickensian that was the doctor's recipe

parts.note: to bath is to wash
Oliver Twist is the young hero of the Dickens novel

explanation.surface: Cleaning up Dickens's orphan boy on medical advice.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a dry biscuit created by Dr William Oliver of Bath in the 18th century, hence 'the doctor's recipe'.
explanation.definitionFit: The plain biscuit was devised by an 18th-century physician of the spa town, and named after him.

clue.text: Did be entertain Wordsworth's golden crowd?

definitions.meaning: asks whether he was the one receiving guests
Wordsworth's daffodils poem sees 'a crowd, / A ..., of golden daffodils'

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a man threw a party for the poet's daffodils.
explanation.definitionFit: One who receives guests plays the role of the entertaining party, and the poet calls his mass of daffodils a multitude of that name.

clue.text: Fish tea

definitions.meaning: a fish of the salmon family found in cold lakes
informal British slang for a cup of tea

explanation.definitionFit: Char is a lake fish related to trout, and also British slang from Chinese cha for tea.

clue.text: Where is this sold? Oh, in the local, maybe

definitions.text: Where is this sold? Oh, in the local, maybe

indicators.note: the exclamation sits inside the shuffled word, just as the clue says it is in it
maybe suggests a possible, rearranged version of the letters of local

explanation.surface: Someone asks where a thing is on sale and answers themselves: down at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' is the anagram signal and 'in' the container signal. The whole clue also answers itself: drink is sold in the local, the British term for a neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer, wine and spirits are sold in a pub, and the intoxicating ingredient they share names them collectively.

clue.text: Mark is angry after a battle perhaps

parts.note: a scar is a mark left on the skin
red can mean angry, as in seeing red

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark is furious once a fight is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a name; it is the wound's trace, and 'is' only links it to RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier may come out of combat marked with healed wounds, so the adjective describes the state after battle.

clue.text: The colour of the song maiden, ripe Hazel

definitions.text: The colour of the song maiden
definitions.meaning: the old English ballad of the '... Maid' names her by her colour
a hazel's fruit when ripe has a warm brown shell

explanation.surface: Describing the shade of a ballad's girl, a mature woman named Hazel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazel' looks like a woman's name; it is the tree whose ripe fruit gives the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad heroine is called after her complexion, and a ripened hazel nut has exactly that warm brown shade.

clue.text: Get in the way of multi-footed creature?

definitions.meaning: a joke on centipede: the word ends in -pede, Latin for feet, as if it were a creature

explanation.surface: Obstructing a many-legged insect crossing the path.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: the word looks as if it belongs with centipede and millipede, whose endings mean feet.
explanation.definitionFit: To impede is to hinder progress, and its ending matches the Latin foot element in names of many-legged bugs.
